[PATH:empirical] Project STAR (Student/Teacher Achievement Ratio) longitudinal data re-analysis — This landmark randomized controlled trial provides direct evidence on class size reduction effects in early elementary grades. Re-analyzing its data with modern statistical methods can confirm effect sizes and heterogeneity by socioeconomic status.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analyses of class size interventions (e.g., Hattie, Biddle & Berliner) — Systematic reviews and meta-analyses consolidate findings across multiple studies, allowing assessment of overall effect direction, magnitude, and moderators like student disadvantage, thus disputing or corroborating the hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Causal inference from administrative dataset (e.g., regression discontinuity using state-level class-size caps) — Natural experiments arising from policy-induced class size thresholds near caps offer quasi-experimental evidence on literacy and numeracy gains, particularly for disadvantaged students, providing real-world counter-evidence to experimental findings.

[PATH:empirical] Project STAR (Student/Teacher Achievement Ratio) longitudinal data, re-analyzed for secondary school outcomes — Project STAR is a landmark randomized experiment on class size in early grades; re-analyzing its long-term follow-up data for secondary school test scores can provide causal evidence on sustained effects.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of class size reduction interventions in secondary schools from the Campbell Collaboration or What Works Clearinghouse — A systematic review and meta-analysis of existing quasi-experimental and experimental studies can aggregate effect sizes and assess heterogeneity, especially regarding moderators like teacher quality and curriculum.

[PATH:empirical] Natural experiment using variation in school funding policies that reduce class sizes in secondary schools, with administrative data on test scores and teacher characteristics — Exploiting exogenous variation from policy changes (e.g., class size mandates or funding formula shifts) allows estimation of causal effects while controlling for confounding factors such as teacher quality and curriculum intensity.
